chunks: My father, may Allah be pleased with him, said in his letter to me:
Know, O my son, that the ruling concerning all claims is that the proof is upon the claimant, and the oath is upon the one against whom the claim is made.

So if he refuses the oath, the claim becomes binding upon him. And if the defendant returns the oath to the claimant, when the claimant does not have two witnesses, and he does not swear, then there is no right for him.

Except in the prescribed punishments, for there is no oath in them; and in blood cases, the proof is upon the defendant and the oath is upon the claimant, lest the blood of a Muslim person be nullified.

key_terms.الدَّعَاوِي: formal claims or disputes brought before judgment
key_terms.الدَّمِ: cases involving bloodshed, homicide, or bodily injury
key_terms.الْبَيِّنَةَ: proof or evidentiary support required from the claimant
key_terms.الْحُدُودِ: the prescribed penal limits in which oath is not applied here
key_terms.الْحُكْمَ: the legal ruling or judicial principle being stated
key_terms.الْمُدَّعَى عَلَيْهِ: the defendant, against whom the claim is brought
key_terms.الْمُدَّعِي: the claimant who initiates the legal claim
key_terms.الْيَمِينَ: the oath used in judicial procedure

ai.seo_question: What is the rule of evidence and oath in Islamic legal claims and blood cases?
ai.summary: This report lays out a foundational legal principle in adjudicating claims: the claimant must produce evidence, while the defendant may clear himself by oath. It also explains exceptions in hudud and blood cases, highlighting the special gravity of criminal punishments and the protection of Muslim life in judicial procedure.
